items.title: 50-year old with chest pain: serial ECG 'STEMI negative'
items.summary: A signed-off 'STEMI negative' tracing with a down/up inferior T wave, an akinetic apex on bedside echo, and a troponin that climbed from 1,665 to 21,018 ng/L.
items.note: The ECG looked more ischaemic as the pain improved, which is exactly the trap the OMI paradigm exists to catch — and the thing that gets argued about when you ring the cath lab without ST elevation to point at. The bedside echo is what settles it here: extensive regional dysfunction across the apex and mid-to-distal anterior, lateral and septal walls, which is CCPU territory and the reason the probe belongs in that conversation. Dr Smith's blog is new to this feed and is the closest thing going to a dedicated ECG teaching case series, so it is worth adding to the rotation alongside the LITFL ECG cases.

items.title: Episode 227: Diarrhea
items.summary: When stool testing actually changes anything in acute diarrhoea, and a spotlight on Cyclospora you will otherwise never think of.
items.note: Acute diarrhoea is the presentation where the reflex is to send a panel and move on, and this is a concise argument about which patients that helps and which it just delays. The Cyclospora section is the part worth keeping — it is the organism that sits outside the usual differential until someone names it. Follows episode 226 on superwarfarin toxicity, already in the feed.

items.title: The 103rd Bubble Wrap x Wrexham Park Hospital
items.summary: Five papers, three of which land directly on decisions made in a mixed ED: bronchiolitis monitoring, URTIs before sedation, and antibiotics for appendicitis.
items.note: The procedural sedation question is the useful one — whether a child's current URTI should delay sedation is the argument that happens at the bedside with no evidence usually quoted, and here it is quoted. The continuous-versus-intermittent pulse oximetry paper in bronchiolitis matters for the same reason, since the monitor drives admission as much as the child does. The Bubble Wrap format is five appraisals by trainees in about ten minutes of reading, which makes it a better use of a gap than most journal clubs.

items.title: RCH investigating chemical exposure risk after glove bungle
items.summary: Clinicians at Victoria's paediatric referral hospital gave chemotherapy in gloves never rated for cytotoxics, possibly for a decade.
items.note: The specific failure is a standard — ASTM D6978-05, the permeation test that makes a glove a chemo glove — and nobody checked the sterile gloves against it, even after parts of the hospital stopped using them ten years ago. WorkSafe raised it in August; the hospital has now commissioned independent testing. It is a reminder worth having that the PPE handed to you in a public hospital is rated for something, and that it is worth knowing what.

items.title: Ebola death toll in Congo tops 4,000
items.summary: 4,018 deaths from 8,300 cases since May — now the second-largest and fastest-growing Ebola outbreak recorded.
items.note: The reason this one keeps escalating is in the species: Bundibugyo, not Zaire, so the licensed vaccine and the two approved monoclonals do not apply and candidates are still being tested mid-outbreak. That is the detail the headline numbers bury, and it is why the growth curve looks nothing like 2018-20. The feed has been tracking this since the WHO DON notices and the ABC case-number graphs in August; this is where it has got to.

items.title: Surprise Chef's Frogs In A Pond Out October 23
items.summary: Melbourne's own cinematic soul-funk quartet cut a continuous 40-minute suite live over nine days, with Leon Michels on flute.
items.note: Leon Michels is the thread back to the shelf — El Michels Affair, Big Crown, the Menahan Street Band and Sharon Jones orbit — and here he is playing flute on a record made in Melbourne. The method is the interesting part: one continuous suite rather than tracks, recorded live across a nine-day session with minimal overdubbing, built off Italian giallo scoring rather than the usual Daptone reference points. Out 23 October, which is enough notice to have it ordered.

items.title: Kribo Records: a Singaporean home for classic funk and soul
items.summary: A one-man label built explicitly on the Daptone and Big Crown model, except the owner plays every note on every release himself.
items.note: Haqim Isa cites Daptone and Big Crown as the template — both already represented on the shelf and in this feed — then does something neither does, recording everything himself in his own studio under pseudonyms. The twist that makes it worth hearing rather than just admiring is the instrumentation: sitar and electric phin, vocals in Malay, a deliberate 'Nusantara sound' laid over wah-wah, Rhodes and heavy drums. Good company for the Colemine and Mainstream label guides already published.

items.title: New website aims to list every film camera ever made
items.summary: Camera Index has launched with 1,400-odd cameras under 'A' alone, which tells you both how useful and how mad the project is.
items.note: Reference material for film cameras is scattered across dead forums, one-man sites and eBay listings, so a single index with a real taxonomy is genuinely worth something when you are checking what a shutter speed range or a lens mount should be. Starting at 'A' with 1,400 entries sets the scale of the thing honestly. Pairs with the Braun Paxette and Zeiss 342 reviews already in the feed — the obscure end is exactly where an index earns its keep.

items.title: My Favorite Photo – a One Shot Story
items.summary: Christopher Welch on the frame that got him shooting black and white again after a thirty-five year gap, on the Oregon coast.
items.note: The One Shot Story format is the best thing 35mmc does — one picture, the circumstances, and why it stuck — and this one is about returning to film after a single college class in 1991. The Tillamook and Cannon Beach drive is incidental; the useful part is how little equipment and how much intent the picture needed. Sits beside the other One Shot Stories already in the feed.

items.title: Introducing Hidden Forts: A World of Its Own
items.summary: The man who introduced America to Japanese denim through Blue in Green has started his own label, all Japanese components, made in Japan.
items.note: Gordon Heffner co-founded Blue in Green in Soho, which is a large part of why anyone outside Japan knows Samurai, Warehouse or Oni by name — Heddels interviewed him about it back in 2013. 'Rugged Nostalgia' is a label line, but the provenance underneath it is real: Japanese components throughout, handcrafted in Japan, $365 at Division Road with one-wash variants direct. Worth watching rather than buying from Australia yet, but this is the vintage-rustic end done by someone who knows where the cloth comes from.

items.title: Dragonwilds Update 1.000.007 Fixes Save Issues
items.summary: The patch that finally stops multiplayer world-hopping eating your inventory and quest progress — and the rule it uses to decide which save wins.
items.note: This is the fix for the bug behind the 1.0.0.5 and 1.0.0.6 patches already in the feed: character progress was not carrying between multiplayer worlds. The resolution is worth knowing before you log in, because it is not neutral — the world you have spent the most time in is taken as the true save and overrides on login, so hop deliberately the first time. Also fixes console clients failing to join worlds with two players already in, and save corruption when joining a modded dedicated server.

items.title: Jacket, a Thornbury Jazz Bar Designed From a Playlist
items.summary: A 90-seat High Street room where listening is the point, programmed across funk, soul and jazz by the musician who built it.
items.note: Tamer Taşkaya handed Studio Heck a playlist instead of a brief and let rhythm and tempo drive the fit-out — the designers are musicians themselves, which is why that is not just a press line. The programming is the reason to go: live jazz trios through the week, soul and funk DJs, flamenco nights, and a stated intention that the music not be intimidating. Eight minutes from the Thornbury Crawl route already in the feed, and the closest thing northside has to the listening-bar sensibility the record shelf keeps circling.
